revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Puzzle Problem
revealWordProblem.text:
The percentage of each type of puzzle in a toy store before a sale is shown. During the sale, the store sold all of its 300-piece and 500-piece puzzles — 120 puzzles in all.
Question: How many of each type of puzzle did the store have before the sale?
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: A picture graph of puzzle stock by type: 300-piece 40%, 500-piece 35%, 750-piece 15%, and 1,000-piece 10%.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The puzzles that sold were the 300-piece and 500-piece stock together: 40% + 35% = 75% of the whole stock. So 120 is 75% of the total: 0.75t = 120, giving t = 160 puzzles before the sale. Now take each percent of 160 — 300-piece: 40% of 160 = 64; 500-piece: 35% of 160 = 56; 750-piece: 15% of 160 = 24; 1,000-piece: 10% of 160 = 16. Check: 64 + 56 = 120 sold, and 64 + 56 + 24 + 16 = 160.

reviewHighlights.rule: Finding the Whole Given Part & Percent
steps: 1. Identify the given part and the percentage it represents
2. Convert the percent to a decimal or fraction
3. Divide the part by the percent decimal to find the total whole (100%)
reviewHighlights.watchOut: A common mistake when finding the whole is multiplying by the percent instead of dividing. For "$42 is 60% of the original price," computing 0.6 × 42 = $25.20 makes the original price SMALLER than the sale price — impossible for a discount. Since percent × whole = part, the whole is found by dividing: 42 ÷ 0.6 = $70. Whenever the percent is less than 100%, the whole must come out larger than the part, so a smaller answer is the tell.

level3.stem: A toy store's puzzle stock was 25% 300-piece, 15% 500-piece, and the rest 1,000-piece. During a sale the store sold ALL of its 300-piece and 500-piece puzzles — 120 puzzles in total. How many of each type did the store have before the sale? Explain your reasoning.
level3.sampleAnswer: The 120 puzzles sold were the 300-piece and 500-piece stock together, so they represent 25% + 15% = 40% of the whole stock. That makes 120 the part and 40% the percent, with the total stock unknown: 0.4t = 120, so t = 120 ÷ 0.4 = 300 puzzles in all. Now find each type as a part of that whole: 300-piece = 0.25 × 300 = 75 puzzles, 500-piece = 0.15 × 300 = 45 puzzles, and 1,000-piece = the remaining 60% = 0.6 × 300 = 180 puzzles. Check: 75 + 45 = 120 sold ✓, and 75 + 45 + 180 = 300 ✓.
hints: What percent of the stock did the 120 sold puzzles make up?
Add the two percents before you divide.
0.4t = 120 — then use the whole to find each type.

level3.stem: A shop reports that this week's $60 in sales is 120% of last week's. Was last week better or worse, and by how much?
choices: Worse — last week was $50, so sales rose by $10
Better — last week was $72, so sales fell
Worse — last week was $48
You cannot tell without knowing the number of items sold
level3.explanation: Last week is the whole here, so last week is 100%. This week's $60 stands for 120% of last week. Divide to find the whole: 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50. Last week was $50, so sales rose by $10.
choiceFeedback: That takes 120% OF 60. Here 60 is already the 120%, so you divide rather than multiply.
That subtracts 20% of 60. The 20% is measured against last week, not this week.
The percent relationship is enough — item counts are not needed.
hints: Which number is the whole here, this week or last week?
$60 stands for 120%, so what does 100% stand for?
Divide 60 by 1.2.
level3.stemEs: Una tienda informa que los $60 de ventas de esta semana son el 120% de los de la semana pasada. ¿Fue mejor o peor la semana pasada, y por cuánto?
choicesEs: Peor — la semana pasada fue $50, así que las ventas subieron $10
Mejor — la semana pasada fue $72, así que las ventas bajaron
Peor — la semana pasada fue $48

level3.explanationEs: La semana pasada es el todo aquí, así que la semana pasada es el 100%. Los $60 de esta semana representan el 120% de la semana pasada. Divide para hallar el todo: 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50. La semana pasada fueron $50, así que las ventas subieron $10.
hintsEs: ¿Cuál número es el entero aquí, esta semana o la pasada?

level3.stem: To find the whole when $9 is 25% of it, Lena divides 9 by 0.25. Omar reasons that 25% is a quarter, so he multiplies 9 by 4. Whose method works?
choices: Both — dividing by 0.25 and multiplying by 4 are the same operation
Only Lena — multiplying cannot undo a percent
Only Omar — you should never divide by a decimal
Neither — you need the whole before you can use either method
level3.explanation: 25% is the same as one quarter. Dividing by 0.25 asks how many quarters fit into 9. Multiplying by 4 answers that same question directly. Both routes give the same whole: 9 × 4 = 36.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying by 4 undoes taking a quarter — that is exactly what is needed.
Dividing by a decimal is a normal operation and gives the same answer here.
The part and the percent are enough; the whole is what you are finding.
hints: What fraction is 25%?
Work out 9 ÷ 0.25 and 9 × 4 and compare them.
If two methods agree every time, what does that say about them?
level3.stemEs: Para hallar el entero cuando $9 es el 25% de él, Lena divide 9 entre 0.25. Omar razona que el 25% es un cuarto, así que multiplica 9 por 4. ¿El método de quién funciona?
choicesEs: Los dos — dividir entre 0.25 y multiplicar por 4 son la misma operación
Solo el de Lena — multiplicar no puede deshacer un porcentaje
Solo el de Omar — nunca se debe dividir entre un decimal
Ninguno — necesitas el entero antes de usar cualquiera de los dos métodos
level3.explanationEs: El 25% es lo mismo que un cuarto. Dividir entre 0.25 pregunta cuántos cuartos caben en 9. Multiplicar por 4 responde esa misma pregunta directamente. Los dos caminos dan el mismo todo: 9 × 4 = 36.
hintsEs: ¿Qué fracción es el 25%?
Calcula 9 ÷ 0.25 y 9 × 4 y compáralos.
Si dos métodos coinciden siempre, ¿qué dice eso de ellos?

level3.stem: Claim: “If the percent is less than 100, the whole is always bigger than the part.” Always, sometimes, or never true?
choices: Always — a percent under 100 describes less than one whole, so the whole must be larger
Sometimes — it depends whether the numbers are money or counts
Never — the part and the whole are always equal
Sometimes — it fails when the percent is under 10
level3.explanation: 100% means the part and the whole are the same size. A percent below 100 means the part covers less than all of it. So the whole has to be the larger of the two numbers. For example, $9 is 25% of 36.
choiceFeedback: What the numbers measure makes no difference — the relationship is about the percent.
They are equal only at exactly 100%.
Try 5%: $5 is 5% of $100, and the whole is far larger.
hints: What does 100% mean about the part and the whole?

level3.stemEs: Afirmación: “Si el porcentaje es menor que 100, el entero siempre es mayor que la parte.” ¿Siempre, a veces o nunca es cierto?
choicesEs: Siempre — un porcentaje menor que 100 describe menos de un entero, así que el entero tiene que ser mayor
A veces — depende de si los números son dinero o conteos
Nunca — la parte y el entero siempre son iguales
A veces — falla cuando el porcentaje es menor que 10
level3.explanationEs: El 100% significa que la parte y el todo son del mismo tamaño. Un porcentaje menor que 100 significa que la parte cubre menos que el total. Así que el todo tiene que ser el mayor de los dos números. Por ejemplo, $9 es el 25% de 36.
hintsEs: ¿Qué dice el 100% sobre la parte y el entero?
Si la parte es menor que el entero, ¿cuál número es mayor?
Prueba un porcentaje pequeño y uno justo por debajo de 100.
